title: Holy Bread and a Giant's Sword
sum: David, now running for his life, comes alone to Nob, the town of the priests. He tells Ahimelech the priest that he is on a secret mission for the king, and asks for bread. The only bread is the holy Presence Bread, which Ahimelech gives him once David assures him his men are ritually clean. David also takes the sword of Goliath, kept at the sanctuary as a trophy. One of Saul's men, Doeg the Edomite, sees it all.

David then flees to Achish, king of Gath, Goliath's own city. The king's servants recognize him as the hero of the women's song, and David, terrified, pretends to be insane. He scratches on the gate and drools into his beard, and Achish sends him away in disgust. The chapter shows the anointed king at his lowest: lying, hungry, and acting mad among his enemies, with Goliath's own sword at his side.
readings: Read as the start of the fugitive years

Chapters 21–31 follow David from the moment he leaves Saul's court to the day Saul dies. This chapter sets the pattern: David survives by his wits, but his choices have costs for others. The lie to Ahimelech will cost eighty-five priests their lives (22:18).
Read with the Psalms

Two psalm headings tie psalms to this chapter: Psalm 34 ("when he disguised his good sense before Abimelech") and Psalm 56 ("when the Philistines seized him in Gath"). Read with them, the madman at the gate becomes a man praying under his breath, and the scene becomes a story of rescue.

views.H: David's flight to Nob and Gath came a few years before Saul's death (about 1010 BC). Nob was the sanctuary town of Eli's descendants after Shiloh; Gath (Tell es-Safi) was a major Philistine city in this period, as excavations show.
views.C: Many critical scholars think the Gath episode (21:10–15) is a separate tradition from David's longer stay with Achish in chapter 27, and some see the whole flight story as part of an "apology" for David, explaining away his time among the Philistines.
views.L: Literary readers note the reversals: the giant-killer carries the giant's sword into the giant's city and must play the fool to survive. Doeg is planted silently in 21:7, to speak in 22:9.
views.J: The Talmud discusses whether the day was a Sabbath and teaches that danger to life overrides the law about holy bread (Menachot 95b). The Midrash on Psalms tells how David learned in Gath why God created madness.
views.X: Jesus cites David eating the holy bread to defend his hungry disciples on the Sabbath (Mark 2:25–26). The "Son of David" claims the same freedom, and more: he is Lord of the Sabbath.

deep.b: In Mark, Jesus says David entered God's house "while Abiathar was high priest" (Mark 2:26). In 1 Samuel the priest is Ahimelech; Abiathar is his son, who escapes the massacre (22:20). Matthew and Luke leave out the name. Explanations include: Mark's Greek can mean "in the passage about Abiathar," the way Jesus says "at the bush" for the passage about the burning bush (Mark 12:26); the names of father and son are interchanged elsewhere (2 Samuel 8:17; 1 Chronicles 18:16; 24:6), so tradition may have known both; Abiathar, as the better-known priest of David's reign, may be named for the period. Many critical scholars simply call it a slip, by Jesus or by Mark. The point of the citation does not depend on the name: human need can come before a ritual rule.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the two things David takes from Nob
deep.b: This is my own reading. David leaves Nob with two things: holy bread and Goliath's sword. One stands for God's provision, the other for David's own strength and fame. Saul's court hears of both: Doeg reports the sword (22:10), and Saul charges Ahimelech with giving David "bread and a sword" (22:13). But David never uses the sword. In Gath it is useless, and he survives by giving up every sign of strength. In the chapters that follow he lives by what God provides, and the giant's sword is not mentioned again after 22:13. Commentators note the irony of carrying Goliath's sword into Gath; reading the pair as a choice between two ways of living is my own suggestion.

echoes: Leviticus 24:5–9; Exodus 25:30; Mark 2:23–28; Matthew 12:1–8; Luke 6:1–5; Psalm 34; Psalm 56; 17:51; 18:7; 22:9–19

settings.what: David asks for bread at Nob
settings.to: Ahimelech the priest at Nob
settings.when: while David is running from Saul, with Doeg the Edomite watching
settings.why: David lies that he is on the king's secret business and asks for bread and a weapon. The priest gives him the holy Presence Bread and Goliath's sword. The lie has deadly results, as David himself admits (22:22). Jesus used the story to show that human need can come before ritual rules (Mark 2:25–26).
views: Some readers think he lied to protect the priest from knowing too much. Others note that he takes the blame afterward, and see the story as one of the book's honest portraits of David's faults.

settings.what: David plays the madman at Gath
settings.by: the servants of Achish, then Achish king of Gath
settings.to: Achish, then his servants
settings.when: when David first runs from Saul to the Philistine city of Gath
settings.why: The servants recognize David as the hero of the women's song. Frightened, David pretends to be mad, and Achish asks why they brought him a madman. The scene shows how low David fell, and how he saved his life by his wits. The heading of Psalm 34 links that psalm to this event.

title: The Massacre at Nob
sum: David hides in the cave of Adullam, and about four hundred men gather to him: the desperate, the indebted and the bitter. He leaves his parents in the care of the king of Moab, and the prophet Gad sends him back into Judah.

Meanwhile Saul sits under a tamarisk at Gibeah and accuses his own servants of plotting with David. Doeg the Edomite reports what he saw at Nob. Saul summons Ahimelech and all the priests, refuses to hear the priest's honest defense, and orders them killed. His own guards refuse; Doeg obeys. Eighty-five priests die, and Nob is wiped out, people and animals alike. One son, Abiathar, escapes to David, who admits that he is to blame. The chapter marks Saul's lowest act and David's gain of a priest and an ephod.
readings: Read as a study of tyranny

Saul's speech shows how a frightened ruler sees conspiracies everywhere, rewards his own tribe, and treats loyalty as treason. The refusal of his guards and the brave words of Ahimelech stand out against it.
Read as fulfilled prophecy

The man of God had warned Eli that his house would be cut down, with one survivor (2:31–33). Nob's priests are Eli's descendants, and Abiathar is the one left. The narrator does not say they deserved it; he shows an old word coming true through an unjust king.

views.H: The massacre is a historical event; its memory survives in Psalm 52's heading and in Abiathar's career as David's priest.
views.C: Critical scholars note how the story serves David's later claim: Saul destroyed the priesthood, and David protected its survivor. Some see the account shaped to explain why Abiathar's line served David.
views.L: The list "man and woman, child and nursing baby, ox, donkey and sheep" repeats the order Saul failed to carry out against Amalek (15:3). The king who would not destroy Israel's enemy destroys God's priests.
views.J: The rabbis made Doeg the model of the evil tongue: his report killed the speaker, the hearer and the one spoken of (Arakhin 15b), and the Mishnah denies him a share in the world to come (Sanhedrin 10:2).
views.X: Christian readers have seen David's band of the distressed as a picture of the church gathered around a rejected king, and Abiathar's flight to David as the move from a failing order to the true anointed one.

deep.b: Saul's speech (22:7–8) is the clearest picture in the book of how his kingship works. He sits under a tree with his spear, surrounded by Benjaminites. He asks whether David will give them "fields and vineyards" and make them commanders, assuming that loyalty is bought. He accuses them all of conspiracy, and blames his son. He never says David's name. Samuel had warned that a king would take and give in exactly this way (8:11–17). By the end of the chapter, the king of Israel has used a foreigner to kill Israel's priests. The guards' refusal (22:17) is the first sign that Saul's own people will not follow him everywhere.

The heading ties Psalm 52 to Doeg's report. The psalm begins, "Why do you boast in evil, mighty man?" and accuses the tongue that "plots ruin like a sharpened razor." It ends with the speaker as "a leafy olive tree in God's house," trusting God's loyal love. Whether or not David wrote it on this occasion, the editors who added the heading saw in this chapter a clash between a destructive tongue and God's house, and they were right to see it.

settings.to: David, at the stronghold
settings.when: after David has left his parents with the king of Moab
settings.why: The prophet tells David to leave the stronghold and go into Judah. It is the first time Gad appears. The word shows that David, unlike Saul, has a prophet guiding him, and that his place is among his own people of Judah.

settings.to: his servants, the men of Benjamin, at Gibeah
settings.when: when he hears David has been seen with his men
settings.why: Saul asks whether the son of Jesse will give them fields and posts, and accuses them all of plotting with Jonathan against him. He speaks as a tribal chief buying loyalty from his own tribe. The speech shows his fear turning to suspicion, and it leads Doeg to betray the priests.

settings.to: King Saul, at Gibeah
settings.when: when Saul accuses him and his family of plotting with David
settings.why: Ahimelech says honestly that no one is more loyal than David, the king's son-in-law and captain of his guard, and that he knew nothing of any quarrel. Saul orders the priests killed anyway, and only the Edomite Doeg will do it. The fulfillment of the oracle against Eli's house (2:31–33) comes through Saul's injustice.

settings.to: Abiathar, the only priest of Nob to escape
settings.when: after Abiathar brings word of the massacre
settings.why: David admits that he caused the deaths, because he knew Doeg would report him. He promises Abiathar safety. From now on David has a priest with the ephod to ask God's will. Saul has killed his own priests, and he will soon find that God does not answer him (28:6).

title: Asking the LORD
sum: Hearing that the Philistines are raiding Keilah, David asks the LORD whether to fight, asks again when his men are afraid, and saves the town. Abiathar's arrival with the ephod gives David a way to ask God directly. When Saul plans to trap David in Keilah, David asks whether the townspeople will hand him over. The answer is yes, so he leaves.

In the wilderness of Ziph, Jonathan comes to David one last time, strengthens his hand in God, and says plainly that David will be king and he himself will stand second. The Ziphites betray David to Saul, who closes in at the wilderness of Maon. As Saul's men surround the mountain, a messenger brings news of a Philistine raid, and Saul turns back. The place is named Sela-hammahlekoth, the Rock of Parting.
readings: Read as two kinds of asking

David asks God through the ephod and gets clear answers (23:2, 4, 11–12). Saul, whose name means "asked," relies on informers. The chapter sets up the contrast that will end at Endor, where Saul asks a dead man.
Read as providence

The narrator's verdict, "God never put him into Saul's hands" (23:14), stands over the whole chapter. The Philistine raid that saves David at the last minute is not called a miracle, but the reader is meant to see God's hand in it.

views.H: The places can be located: Keilah (Khirbet Qila), Ziph (Tell Zif), Maon and the Judean Desert east of them. The story fits a real outlaw's life in that country.
views.C: Critical scholars note that 23:19–24:22 and 26:1–25 seem to be two versions of a similar tradition, and that the Ziphite betrayal appears in both.
views.L: "Hand" is the key word: Saul claims God has given David into his hand, Jonathan says Saul's hand will not find him, and the narrator says God never put him into Saul's hands.
views.J: The love of David and Jonathan is the Mishnah's example of love that does not depend on gain (Avot 5:16). Radak reads God's answers about Keilah as conditional on David staying.
views.X: Theologians cite 23:10–13 for God's knowledge of what would happen under other conditions ("middle knowledge"). Jonathan's self-giving has been compared to John the Baptist's (John 3:30).

deep.b: Jonathan's words at Horesh (23:17) are the clearest statement in Saul's family that David will be king. He gives up his own claim, hoping only to stand beside David. The covenant the two make "before the LORD" (23:18) renews the one in 20:12–17, which included a promise to protect Jonathan's family. They never meet again. Jonathan dies at Gilboa (31:2), and David keeps the promise to his son Mephibosheth (2 Samuel 9). Jonathan's last act for David is to make his hand strong in God, and when David is utterly alone at Ziklag, that is exactly what he does for himself (30:6).

Psalm 54's heading ties it to the Ziphites' betrayal (23:19; 26:1). The psalm prays, "By your name, O God, rescue me," and complains that "outsiders have stood up against me, and brutal men are hunting for my life" (Psalm 54:1, 3). The Ziphites were men of Judah, so "outsiders" fits them only in a moral sense, as people who acted like foreigners. The psalm ends in thanks for rescue, which fits the escape at the Rock of Parting.

settings.what: The LORD sends David to Keilah
settings.to: the LORD, and David's men
settings.when: when the Philistines raid Keilah's threshing floors
settings.why: David asks God twice whether to fight, because his men are afraid. God tells him to go and promises victory. David acts as a true king should, rescuing a town of Judah, and he does it by asking the LORD first, as Saul did not.

settings.to: the LORD, God of Israel, through Abiathar's ephod
settings.when: when David hears Saul is coming to besiege Keilah
settings.why: David asks whether Saul will come and whether the people of Keilah will hand him over. God answers yes to both, and David leaves. The answers show God protecting David, and readers see that those he rescues may still betray him.

settings.to: David, at Horesh in the wilderness of Ziph
settings.when: while Saul is hunting David
settings.why: Jonathan tells David not to fear, because he will be king over Israel with Jonathan second to him, "Saul my father knows it too." These are Jonathan's last recorded words to David. The heir to the throne names David as king, which answers anyone who claimed David took the throne from Saul's family.

title: The Edge of the Robe
sum: Saul takes three thousand men to En-gedi to hunt David. He steps into a cave to relieve himself, not knowing that David and his men are hiding in the back of it. David's men urge him to strike: this is the day God promised. David cuts off the edge of Saul's robe instead, and even that troubles his conscience. He will not lift his hand against "the LORD's anointed."

When Saul leaves, David calls after him, bows to the ground, holds up the piece of robe, and pleads his innocence. Let the LORD judge between us, he says. Saul weeps, calls David "my son," admits that David is in the right and will surely be king, and asks him to swear not to wipe out his descendants. David swears, and they part.
readings: Read as a test of restraint
Everything favors killing Saul: the opportunity, the men's urging, even a claimed word from God. David's restraint shows that he will receive the kingdom, not take it.
Read as a royal apology

Many critical scholars see chapters 24 and 26 as part of a defense of David: whatever was said about him, he never raised a hand against Saul, and even Saul admitted David's right to the throne (24:20).

views.H: The caves of En-gedi and the sheepfolds at their mouths fit the setting exactly. Traditional readers take the event as history and the speech as David's own.
views.C: Chapter 24 and chapter 26 are often seen as two versions of one tradition. Both make Saul confess David's innocence and future kingship, a theme typical of a document defending David.
views.L: The robe's edge recalls 15:27–28, where Saul tore Samuel's robe and lost the kingdom. Saul's "Is this your voice, my son David?" will be repeated word for word in 26:17.
views.J: The Talmud says David was punished for disrespecting Saul's garment: in old age, clothes could not warm him (Berakhot 62b; 1 Kings 1:1). David's restraint is a model of honoring authority even in an enemy.
views.X: Christians have read David's refusal to take revenge as an Old Testament picture of loving one's enemy (Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:19–21), and the heading of Psalm 57, "in the cave," as the prayer behind it.

deep.b: David's phrase for Saul, meshiach YHWH, is the root of the word "Messiah." In 1 Samuel it simply means the king God chose and had anointed with oil. David uses it as the reason he will not kill Saul: the office belongs to God. Later Israel applied the title to a hoped-for king from David's line (Psalm 2:2), and Christians to Jesus. In the 1600s, kings used David's words to claim that subjects may never resist them; their opponents answered that David armed himself and fled, which is resistance, while still refusing murder. The text itself is about David's personal restraint, not a general rule for every ruler.

Two psalms are headed "in the cave." Psalm 57 asks for shelter "in the shadow of your wings until the ruin has gone by" and ends with praise: "Be exalted above the heavens, God" (Psalm 57:5, 11). Psalm 142 is a lonely cry: no one cares for my life, "bring me out of prison" (Psalm 142:4, 7). One cave may be Adullam (22:1) and the other En-gedi, or both may refer to this scene. The headings are probably later than the psalms, but they show that early Jewish readers heard David's cave as a place of prayer.

The edge of a robe appears in three scenes that form a sequence. In 15:27, Saul tears Samuel's robe, and Samuel says the kingdom is torn from him. In 24:4, David cuts Saul's robe, and Saul then admits the kingdom will be David's (24:20). In 28:14, Saul recognizes Samuel by his robe and hears the kingdom given to David by name (28:17). Each time a robe is torn or seen, the kingdom moves one step from Saul to David. Robert Polzin traces this me'il motif from Samuel's childhood robe (2:19) to Endor, and Robert Alter makes the same connection in his notes on 24:4 and 28:14.

echoes: 15:27–28; 26:1–25; Genesis 38:26; Psalm 57; Psalm 142; Matthew 5:44; Romans 12:17–21; 1 Kings 1:1; 2 Samuel 9:1–13; 2 Samuel 21:7

settings.to: King Saul, outside the cave near En-gedi
settings.when: after David cuts off the edge of Saul's robe but spares his life
settings.why: David holds up the piece of the robe as proof that he means Saul no harm. He calls Saul "my father," calls himself a dead dog and a flea, and leaves judgment to the LORD. The speech is meant to persuade Saul, and anyone who heard of it, that David is no rebel. It is a key piece of the case that David never raised his hand against "the LORD's anointed."

settings.to: David
settings.when: after David's speech
settings.why: Saul weeps, says David is more in the right than he, and admits that David will surely be king. He asks David to swear not to wipe out his descendants. Saul's own mouth confirms David's claim. The oath sets up the question of how David will treat Saul's family in 2 Samuel.

traditions.q: David would not harm the LORD's anointed. May Christians ever resist an unjust ruler?
views: The Church of England's Homily against Disobedience (1570) used David's refusal to argue that subjects may never rebel, even against a wicked ruler. Later Anglicans largely gave up the strict divine right of kings.

Calvin taught that private people must suffer, but that lower magistrates have a duty to restrain a tyrant (Institutes 4.20.31). Samuel Rutherford's Lex, Rex (1644) argued that the king is under the law, and answered royalists who cited this chapter.

Luther taught that Christians may not take up arms against their rulers for their own sake, though they must refuse commands to sin (Temporal Authority). Later Lutherans, in the Magdeburg Confession of 1550, held that lower rulers may resist.

Citizens must refuse commands that go against God's law (Catechism 2242). Armed resistance to oppression is allowed only under strict conditions, as a last resort against grave and lasting abuse (Catechism 2243).

Christians never take up the sword, even against a tyrant; they obey God rather than people and accept suffering (Schleitheim Confession, article 6). David's mercy to Saul is read as a picture of the way of the cross.

title: Abigail Stops a Massacre
sum: Samuel dies and is buried in Ramah. Then the story turns to Nabal, a rich and harsh man of Maon whose name means "fool," and his wife Abigail, sensible and beautiful. David's men have protected Nabal's shepherds; at shearing time David asks politely for a share of the feast. Nabal insults him as a runaway slave and sends his men away empty. David straps on his sword and sets out with four hundred men, swearing to leave no male of Nabal's alive.

A servant warns Abigail. She loads donkeys with food and rides out to meet David. Her speech, bold and humble at once, persuades him not to shed innocent blood or save himself by his own hand, and foretells his lasting house. David blesses God for sending her. Nabal, drunk at his feast, hears the news the next morning and suffers a collapse; ten days later the LORD strikes him dead. David marries Abigail.
readings: Read as a mirror of Saul

Set between the two chapters where David spares Saul, Nabal's story shows what David might do to an enemy and what God does instead. Nabal feasts like a king, repays good with evil, and is struck down by God (25:38), as David says God will strike Saul (26:10).
Read as Abigail's story

Abigail is one of the wisest people in Samuel. She acts quickly, takes responsibility, and speaks God's promises to David better than anyone since Samuel. The rabbis counted her among Israel's seven prophetesses.
Read politically
Some historians note that marrying the widow of a wealthy Calebite gave David land and standing around Hebron, where he would first be crowned king (2 Samuel 2:1–4).

views.H: Maon and Carmel are real villages south of Hebron; the shearing feast and the economy of herds fit the region. Traditional readers take the story as history and Abigail as a real woman of faith.
views.C: Jon Levenson and others read the story as history with a political point: David gaining a foothold in Calebite territory. Some, like Baruch Halpern, see in David's demand a protection racket that the story turns into a moral tale.
views.L: The chapter is full of wordplay on Nabal's name (fool, wineskin) and builds a contrast between the fool who "returns me evil in place of good" and the wise woman who brings a "blessing."
views.J: Abigail is one of the seven prophetesses (Megillah 14a) and one of the four most beautiful women (Megillah 15a). Her words "the bundle of the living" became the formula carved on Jewish gravestones.
views.X: Christian readers have seen Abigail as a peacemaker (Matthew 5:9) and an intercessor who takes guilt on herself, and her words as an example of the teaching "make room for the anger" (Romans 12:19).

deep.b: Abigail's speech (25:24–31) is a small masterpiece. She begins by taking the blame (25:24), calls her husband a fool by his own name (25:25), and says she never saw David's messengers (25:25). Then she turns the argument. The LORD has already kept David from bloodguilt (25:26), she says, as if the decision were made. She offers her gift as a "blessing" (25:27). She foretells "a house that stands firm" (25:28), the very promise Nathan will make (2 Samuel 7:16). She pictures David's life safe in God's pouch and his enemies flung away like sling stones, recalling Goliath (25:29). And she gives David a reason to stop that a future king will understand: when you rule, you will not want this blood on your conscience (25:30–31). David hears it as God's own intervention (25:32).

Abigail's phrase tseror hachayyim (25:29) pictured God keeping David safe, perhaps like stones kept in a shepherd's counting pouch. In later Jewish belief it became an image of the soul safe with God after death. The abbreviation of "May his soul be bound up in the bundle of life" appears on Jewish tombstones to this day, and the phrase is part of the memorial prayer El Malei Rachamim. A woman's words to an angry outlaw became the way Jews speak of their dead.

The chapter ends with a list of David's wives (25:42–44): Abigail, Ahinoam of Jezreel, and Michal, whom Saul has given to another man. Jon Levenson and Baruch Halpern proposed that Ahinoam was Saul's own wife of that name (14:50), taken by David as a claim to the throne, as Absalom later took his father's concubines (2 Samuel 16:21–22). Most commentators set the idea aside, chiefly because Saul's Ahinoam was the mother of a grown son, Jonathan, while David's Ahinoam bore his first child years later. The note on 25:43 gives both cases.

deep.title: Claude's theory: Abigail and Hannah
deep.b: This is my own reading. Abigail's role in 1 Samuel matches Hannah's at the start. Both are wise women whose husbands fail to see what is at stake. Elkanah is loving but does not grasp Hannah's grief (1:8); Nabal is a brute who never learns what his wife has done (25:19). The husbands differ sharply, but each woman acts on her own. Both speak of God's power to bring down the proud and raise up the humble: Hannah in her song (2:4–8), Abigail in her picture of the sling (25:29). Both speak of a coming king, Hannah of "his anointed" (2:10) and Abigail of David's lasting house (25:28). Commentators note Abigail's prophetic speech; I am suggesting the narrator placed the two women as matching voices near the beginning and end of 1 Samuel.

settings.to: Nabal, a rich man of Caleb's clan, at his sheep-shearing in Carmel
settings.when: at shearing time, a feast day
settings.why: David greets Nabal with blessings and reminds him that his men protected Nabal's shepherds. He asks for a share of the feast. It is a polite request, but also a claim for payment for protection. Nabal's insulting refusal (25:10–11) sets up the story's test: will David take revenge with his own hand?

settings.to: David, on the road down from the hills, with his four hundred armed men behind him
settings.when: as David rides out to kill every male of Nabal's house
settings.why: Abigail takes the blame, calls her husband a fool, and offers gifts. Then she speaks like a prophet: the LORD will build David a lasting house and make him ruler over Israel, so he must not have needless bloodshed on his conscience. Her words keep the future king from a crime that would stain his reign. She also says out loud the promise later given through Nathan (2 Samuel 7:11–16).
views: A wise woman and a prophetess
Jewish tradition counts Abigail among the seven prophetesses (Bavli Megillah 14a). Many readers praise her as the model of wise speech.
Part of the case for David
Scholars who read the book as royal apology note that the story explains why Nabal died and David married his widow, without David being guilty.

settings.to: Abigail
settings.when: after her plea
settings.why: David blesses the LORD, Abigail and her good sense for keeping him from bloodguilt. His answer shows that he can listen to wise counsel, which Saul and Nabal could not. Ten days later the LORD himself strikes Nabal.

title: The Spear and the Water Jug
sum: The Ziphites betray David again, and Saul comes with three thousand men. This time David goes to Saul. With Abishai he slips into the sleeping camp at night, where Saul lies with his spear stuck in the ground by his head. Abishai begs for one thrust; David refuses. The LORD himself will strike Saul, or he will die naturally or in battle. David takes the spear and water jug instead, and no one wakes, because the LORD had sent a deep sleep on them.

From a distant hilltop David mocks Abner for failing to guard the king, then pleads with Saul. If God has stirred Saul up, let him accept an offering; if men have, let them be cursed, for they are driving David out of the LORD's land. Saul confesses that he has sinned and played the fool, and blesses David. The two part for the last time.
readings: Read as the second test

The chapter repeats chapter 24 with higher stakes. In the cave, Saul came to David by chance; here David goes into Saul's camp on purpose. In the cave he cut a robe; here he could have used Saul's own spear. Between the two stands Nabal, whom God struck.
Read as David's farewell to Israel
David's complaint that he is being driven out of "the LORD's inheritance" (26:19) prepares for chapter 27, where he leaves for Philistia. Saul's blessing is the last word between the two kings.

views.H: Traditional readers see a second, distinct event, noting the many differences from chapter 24 and the progress in Saul's admissions.
views.C: Most critical scholars see a parallel version of the chapter 24 story (both tied to the Ziphites), preserved because each made the same point about David's innocence.
views.L: The spear, Saul's sign throughout, passes into David's hands and is offered back. The deep sleep from the LORD (26:12) is one of the few direct acts of God in these chapters.
views.J: The Talmud quotes 26:19 to teach that whoever lives outside the Land of Israel is like one who has no God (Ketubot 110b). David's refusal to harm a king is a standard example of the duty to honor rulers.
views.X: The verse "Who has ever stretched out his hand against the LORD's anointed?" was central to debates over the divine right of kings, used by royalists and answered by Puritans such as Samuel Rutherford.

deep.b: The two stories share a frame: the Ziphites report David (23:19; 26:1), Saul takes three thousand picked men (24:2; 26:2), Saul is at David's mercy, a companion urges David to kill him (24:4; 26:8), David refuses because Saul is the LORD's anointed (24:6; 26:9), takes a token (robe; spear and jug), calls out from a distance, and Saul answers "Is this your voice, my son David?" and admits his wrong (24:16–17; 26:17, 21). The differences are just as striking: cave and camp, day and night, chance and daring, a robe and a spear. In chapter 24 David's conscience troubles him for cutting a robe; in chapter 26 he does not touch Saul at all. In chapter 24 Saul says David will be king; in chapter 26 he says only that David will succeed. Whether one event told twice or two events, the pair frames Nabal's story and makes the same claim three times: David left judgment to God.

David's complaint in 26:19 shows how closely the land and its God were linked. To be forced into a foreign land meant living among other gods, with no sanctuary of the LORD, no priest, no sacrifice. Naaman's request for Israelite soil (2 Kings 5:17) and the exiles' question in Psalm 137:4 come from the same belief. The prophets later insisted that God was with his people in exile too (Ezekiel 11:16). David's fear is real, and his next step (27:1) is to do the very thing he feared.

settings.what: David forbids killing the LORD's anointed
settings.to: Abishai, standing over the sleeping Saul in his camp
settings.when: at night, when Abishai offers to pin Saul to the ground with one blow
settings.why: David forbids it: no one can harm the LORD's anointed and be innocent. The LORD will strike Saul, or he will die in his time or in battle. For readers, David's restraint answers the charge that he wanted Saul dead. It also states a principle that later kings appealed to.

settings.to: Saul and his army, shouted across from a far hilltop
settings.when: after David has taken Saul's spear and water jug
settings.why: David asks what he has done, and says that those driving him out of the LORD's inheritance are telling him to serve other gods. Saul confesses he has played the fool and blesses David. It is the last time they meet. The speech shows how exile from the land meant exile from the LORD's worship, a fear that later exiles would know well.

title: A Year and Four Months in Philistia
sum: Convinced that Saul will eventually catch him, David takes his six hundred men and their families to Achish king of Gath. Saul stops hunting him. At David's request, Achish gives him the town of Ziklag, which, the narrator notes, has belonged to the kings of Judah ever since.

For sixteen months David raids the desert peoples of the south, the Geshurites, Girzites and Amalekites, leaving no one alive so that no one can report what he is really doing. He tells Achish he has been raiding Judah and its allies. Achish believes him: David has made himself hated by Israel and will be his servant forever.
readings: Read as David's low point

No prophet or ephod guides David's decision. He lives a double life, lies to his host and kills to protect the lie. The chapter ends with Achish completely deceived, and the next chapters bring the reckoning.
Read as shrewd survival
David protects Judah while seeming to attack it, weakens Israel's desert enemies, and gains a town of his own. Many readers see a clever leader doing what he must.

views.H: Ziklag was a real border town; the time in Philistia explains how David later had Philistine soldiers (the Kerethites and Pelethites, and Ittai of Gath) in his service.
views.C: Critical historians often think David really did serve the Philistines as a vassal, and that this chapter and the next explain away an embarrassing fact: he was in the Philistine army when Saul died.
views.L: The narrator reports David's killing and lying without comment, and lets Achish's confident last line (27:12) hang over the coming chapters.
views.J: Jewish commentators debate whether David's raids were justified; many tie them to the command to blot out Amalek (Deuteronomy 25:17–19) and note that he protected Judah.
views.X: Christian commentators have often seen this as a time of faltering faith, comparing Abraham's lies in Egypt and Gerar (Genesis 12; 20), while noting that God kept his promise anyway.

deep.b: Read critically, the facts are stark: David served a Philistine king for over a year, held a town from him, and marched with the Philistine army toward the battle in which Saul died. Many historians, such as Baruch Halpern and Steven McKenzie, think the story in chapters 27–30 was told to answer the charge that David fought for the enemy or had a hand in Saul's death. The text's answer is careful: David only pretended to serve Achish, never attacked Judah, was sent home before the battle, and was fighting Amalekites far to the south when Saul fell. Traditional readers accept that account as true; critical readers see it as true in part and shaped to protect David's name. Both agree the stay in Philistia was the most dangerous moment of David's career, morally as well as physically.

settings.to: David, then Achish
settings.when: during the year and four months David lives at Ziklag under Achish
settings.why: Achish asks whom David raided. David says he raided the Negev of Judah and its clans. In fact he raided Israel's enemies and left no one alive to tell. Achish believes David has made himself hated by his own people. The story answers anyone who said David fought for the Philistines against Judah: he deceived the Philistine king and never harmed his own people.

title: The Medium at Endor
sum: The Philistines gather for war, and Achish tells David he will march with them. Samuel is dead, and Saul has long since removed the mediums from the land. Now, facing the Philistine army camped at Shunem, Saul is terrified. He asks the LORD, but no answer comes by dreams, by the Urim, or by prophets. So he disguises himself, slips around the enemy camp by night, and asks a woman at Endor who has a ghost at her call to bring up Samuel.

She sees Samuel, screams, and realizes her visitor is Saul. She describes an old man coming up out of the earth, wrapped in a robe. Samuel asks why he has been disturbed, and repeats his old verdict: the kingdom has been torn from Saul and given to David because Saul did not carry out God's anger on Amalek. Tomorrow Saul and his sons will be with Samuel, and Israel will fall to the Philistines. Saul collapses. The woman and his servants persuade him to eat, and she serves him a calf and fresh bread before he goes out into the night.
readings: Read as the end of Saul's asking

Saul's name means "asked." He has asked God and been refused; now he asks a dead prophet, through the very practice he had banned, and hears his death. Samuel's "Then why ask me?" (28:16) sums up the whole story.
Read as a ghost story

Taken simply, the chapter is the Bible's fullest scene of a medium raising the dead, with its details of disguise, fear, recognition and a figure rising from the earth. Readers have argued for two thousand years over what really happened.

views.H: Traditional readers usually take the event as real, whether they think Samuel truly appeared or something else did. The geography (Shunem, Gilboa, Endor) fits the night journey exactly.
views.C: Many critical scholars think the scene was placed out of order (the Philistines are at Shunem in 28:4 but still at Aphek in 29:1) to set Saul's doom before David's escape. Some see it as a late addition shaped by the Deuteronomic law against necromancy.
views.L: The chapter mirrors Saul's beginning: he first met Samuel while looking for lost donkeys and was told about his future (chapter 9); now he seeks Samuel again and is told his end. The woman's kindness is the only warmth in Saul's last hours.
views.J: The Talmud says Samuel truly came up, perhaps with Moses (Hagigah 4b), and that Saul's death atoned for him, so that he would be "with" Samuel (Berakhot 12b). Saadia Gaon held that God himself revived Samuel, as Ibn Ezra reports. Samuel ben Hofni argued that the woman deceived Saul; Radak quotes him at length and weighs his view against the sages' tradition.
views.X: Early Christian writers split: Justin Martyr and Origen held that Samuel's soul truly appeared; Tertullian, Eustathius and Gregory of Nyssa said a demon took his form. Luther and Calvin held the demon view; many modern evangelicals hold that God sent the real Samuel.

deep.b:
The case: The narrator says plainly that "the woman saw Samuel" (28:12) and that "Samuel spoke to Saul" (28:15). The figure's words fit Samuel's character and repeat his earlier verdict almost word for word (15:28; 28:17). His prediction comes true the next day (31:1–6), which no medium could arrange. The woman's terrified scream suggests that something happened she did not expect or control. Ancient Jewish readers took it so, and Saadia Gaon later argued that God revived Samuel by a miracle: Sirach says of Samuel, "After he had gone to sleep in death, he still prophesied" (Sirach 46:20), Josephus tells it as a real appearance, and the Talmud discusses it as fact (Hagigah 4b; Shabbat 152b). Among Christians, Justin Martyr used it to show that souls survive death (Dialogue 105), Origen defended it in a homily against those who called it a demon, and Augustine, after hesitating, came to accept that Samuel appeared, citing Sirach.

The strongest form: Most who hold this view today, from Jewish commentators to evangelical scholars such as Robert Bergen and David Tsumura, add that God, not the woman, brought Samuel, as a last word of judgment. That explains her shock: her ritual had barely begun. It also explains why the episode does not endorse necromancy: God overrode it. The law against consulting the dead stands; this was a unique act of God's sovereignty, like Moses and Elijah appearing with Jesus (Matthew 17:3).

deep.h: View 2: It was a demon in Samuel's form
deep.b:
The case: God's law forbids consulting the dead and calls it abhorrent (Deuteronomy 18:10–12). Would God honor a forbidden ritual by sending his prophet? And could a medium have power over a righteous man's soul? Tertullian (On the Soul 57) answered no: a demon imitated Samuel. Eustathius of Antioch wrote a whole treatise against Origen on this point, arguing that the narrator reports appearances from the woman's point of view, and that Satan can disguise himself (2 Corinthians 11:14). Gregory of Nyssa agreed. Luther and Calvin held that it was a devilish illusion meant to drive Saul to despair, and many Protestant interpreters followed them.

The strongest form: Supporters note that the figure offers Saul no call to repent and no hope, only doom; that only the woman sees it; that "a divine being ... rising up out of the earth" (28:13) is the language of underworld spirits; and that 1 Chronicles 10:13 condemns Saul for consulting "a ghost" without saying a prophet answered. A spirit that knew Samuel's past words and could guess the outcome of an unequal battle could deceive with truths.

The case: Only the woman sees anything; Saul only hears, and he hears through her. The Septuagint calls such practitioners "belly-talkers" (engastrimythoi), and the Mishnah says the ba'al ov made voices seem to come from his armpit (Sanhedrin 7:7). Isaiah mocks mediums who "chirp and mutter" from the ground (Isaiah 8:19; 29:4). The woman could have recognized Saul, the tallest man in Israel, with two attendants, asking for Samuel, and the scream could be theater. The message needed no supernatural knowledge: everyone knew Samuel had rejected Saul, and Saul's army was badly outmatched. Samuel ben Hofni, head of the academy at Sura (died 1013), argued that the woman deceived Saul, and the Englishman Reginald Scot (The Discoverie of Witchcraft, 1584) used the passage to argue that "witches" were frauds, not agents of the devil.

The strongest form: Supporters read the narrator's "Samuel said" as reporting the scene as the participants experienced it, as the Bible often does. On this reading, the chapter's point is that Saul, who would not hear God's prophets, ended his life listening to a ventriloquist, and that the true word came anyway, through events.

deep.h: What all three views agree on
deep.b: Every reading agrees that consulting the dead was forbidden (Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:11), that Saul's visit was an act of despair, and that his death followed as Samuel had long warned. Chronicles gives the verdict in one sentence: Saul died for his unfaithfulness, including consulting a ghost (1 Chronicles 10:13–14). The story is not a guide to the afterlife, though it shows that Israel believed the dead continued to exist in some form in Sheol. Jesus' parable of the rich man and Lazarus makes a related point from the other side: a messenger from the dead persuades no one who would not listen to Moses and the prophets (Luke 16:31).

echoes: Leviticus 19:31; Leviticus 20:6; Leviticus 20:27; Deuteronomy 18:9–15; Isaiah 8:19–20; 1 Chronicles 10:13–14; 15:22–28; 9:1–27; Luke 16:19–31; Matthew 17:1–8

settings.by: Samuel, brought up by the medium at Endor
settings.to: King Saul, in disguise, at night
settings.when: the night before the battle on Mount Gilboa, after God has stopped answering Saul
settings.why: Samuel repeats what he said at Gilgal: the LORD has torn the kingdom from Saul and given it to David, because he did not obey about Amalek. Then he adds that tomorrow Saul and his sons will be with him, and Israel's army will fall. Saul's search for a word from God ends with his death sentence. The scene shows readers that the law against consulting the dead (Leviticus 19:31; Deuteronomy 18:10–12) is broken by the very king who enforced it.
views: Many Jewish and Christian readers, and the book itself (28:12, 15), take it that God let Samuel's spirit speak.
Some church fathers, such as Eustathius, argued that the medium or a demon only pretended to be Samuel. Origen answered that the text says Samuel spoke.

traditions.q: Can the faithful dead hear or help the living?
views: The saints are alive in Christ and pray for us, and we may ask for their prayers (Catechism 956, 958), but calling up the dead is forbidden (Catechism 2116–2117). Sirach 46:20, Scripture for Catholics and Orthodox, says Samuel prophesied after his death, so many Catholic teachers hold that God truly sent Samuel.

The Church on earth and in heaven is one, so Orthodox Christians ask the saints to pray for them and pray for the departed. Calling up the dead is forbidden, and the fathers differed over whether Samuel truly appeared.
Scripture does not teach us to call on the saints, but on Christ alone (Augsburg Confession 21). Luther held that the figure at Endor was the devil in Samuel's shape.
Prayer is made to God alone, and not for the dead (Westminster Confession 21.2 and 21.4). Calvin judged that the figure at Endor was a ghostly deception, not Samuel.

The dead sleep and know nothing until the resurrection (Fundamental Beliefs 26; Ecclesiastes 9:5). So the figure at Endor was an evil spirit pretending to be Samuel, and every contact with the dead is a deception.

title: Sent Home from the War
sum: The Philistines muster at Aphek, while Israel camps at the spring in Jezreel. As the Philistine rulers march past with their troops, David and his men bring up the rear with Achish. The Philistine commanders object: "What are these Hebrews?" Achish vouches for David, but the commanders are angry. David could turn against them in the battle, they say, and win back Saul's favor with Philistine heads. Isn't this the David of the women's song?

Achish, swearing by the LORD, tells David he has been upright and is as good as an angel of God in his eyes, but the rulers do not trust him. David protests that he wants to fight "the enemies of my lord the king." Achish sends him back at dawn, and the Philistines go up to Jezreel without him.
readings: Read as a narrow escape
David is spared an impossible choice: fight Saul's army, or betray his host. The suspicion of the Philistine commanders saves him from either.
Read as irony
The pagan king is honest and trusting; David is skilled at deceiving him. David's protest about "my lord the king" can be read two ways, and the narrator does not tell us which he meant.

views.H: The muster at Aphek and the march north to Jezreel fit the Philistines' route up the coastal road. David's dismissal is presented as a real event that kept him from the battle.
views.C: Many historians think the chapter answers the charge that David fought with the Philistines at Gilboa. Its account, that he was sent home before the battle, cannot be checked.
views.L: Achish's warm praise of David ("as good as an angel of God") will be echoed later by David's flatterers in 2 Samuel. The repetition of "good in my eyes" and "not good in the eyes of the rulers" shapes the speech.
views.J: Jewish commentators have usually read David's protest as a ruse: he never meant to fight Israel, and God arranged his release.
views.X: Christian readers have often seen God's providence protecting David from his own compromise, and a lesson that God can rescue his people even from situations they created.

deep.b: Chapter 28 has the Philistines camped at Shunem (28:4), but chapter 29 finds them still mustering at Aphek (29:1), far to the south, and only at the end do they go up to Jezreel (29:11). Chapter 30 then takes three days and more. So the scene at Endor, the night before the battle, takes place after chapter 29 in time. Since David has been back at Ziklag two days when news of the battle arrives (2 Samuel 1:1–2), the night at Endor falls at about the time of chapter 30, while David is chasing the Amalekites. The narrator places it earlier to set Saul's doom alongside David's rescue: on the same days, one king hears his death from a dead prophet, and the other is sent home, asks God, and is answered. The book moves back and forth between the two kings until they meet in death and lament (2 Samuel 1).

settings.what: The Philistine commanders send David away
settings.by: the Philistine commanders, then Achish king of Gath
settings.to: Achish, and then David, at Aphek
settings.when: as the Philistine armies march out to fight Saul at Jezreel
settings.why: The commanders refuse to let David march with them, fearing he will turn on them. Achish praises David as "good as an angel of God" and sends him home. The scene is part of the book's defense of David: he was far away at Ziklag when Saul died, so he had no hand in it.

title: David Strengthens Himself in the LORD
sum: Returning to Ziklag on the third day, David and his men find it burned and their wives and children taken by Amalekite raiders. They weep until they can weep no more, and the men talk of stoning David. But David strengthens himself in the LORD his God, calls for the ephod, and asks whether to pursue. The answer is yes: you will overtake and rescue.

Two hundred exhausted men stay at the Besor wadi. The rest find an Egyptian slave left to die by his Amalekite master, feed him, and follow him to the raiders' camp, where they are feasting. David strikes them from dusk to the next evening and recovers everything and everyone. When some of his men refuse to share the spoil with those who stayed behind, David makes a lasting rule: all share alike. He sends gifts from the spoil to the elders of Judah's towns.
readings: Read against chapter 28
Saul, in crisis, finds God silent and turns to a medium. David, in crisis, turns to God, asks through the ephod, and is answered. The two chapters are a diptych.
Read as the making of a king
David rescues his people, deals justly with the weak, makes law, and shares spoil with Judah's elders. Every act prepares for his anointing at Hebron in 2 Samuel 2.

views.H: The raid fits the life of the Negev, where nomadic raiders on camels struck settled towns. The towns in 30:27–31 are mostly in the hills and south of Judah, the region that will crown David.
views.C: Critical historians see David's gifts as political, building support among Judah's clans, and the chapter as showing David far from Gilboa when Saul died.
views.L: The chapter contrasts the Amalekite who left a sick slave to die with David's men who feed him first and question him later. Small kindness turns the story.
views.J: David's rule on sharing spoil (30:24–25) entered Jewish law as the principle that those who guard the camp share with those who fight.
views.X: Christian preachers have often used 30:6 for the believer alone in crisis, and 30:24 for the value of unseen service in the church.

deep.h: "A rule and a ruling for Israel"
deep.b: David's decision (30:24–25) is the first law in the Bible made by David. Moses had divided the spoil from Midian between the soldiers and the community (Numbers 31:27). David's rule is that all who served share equally, whether in battle or with the baggage. His reason is that the spoil was a gift: "what the LORD has given us" (30:23). The phrase "a rule and a ruling" (chok u-mishpat) is the language of the law of Moses, and "to this day" shows that the rule outlived David. Before he has a throne, David is acting as the lawgiving king Deuteronomy describes (Deuteronomy 17:18–20), and the rule protects the weak against the strong.

settings.what: David asks the LORD through the ephod
settings.to: Abiathar the priest, then the LORD; the LORD answers David
settings.when: at burned Ziklag, when David's men talk of stoning him
settings.why: David asks whether to chase the raiders. God tells him to go after them, and that he will certainly catch them and rescue them all. In the same days, Saul could get no answer from God (28:6). Readers see the difference between the two kings on the eve of Saul's death.

settings.what: David's ruling on sharing the spoil
settings.to: his men, at the Besor wadi, including the worthless men who wanted to keep it all
settings.when: after he rescues the captives and the spoil from the Amalekites
settings.why: David rules that those who stayed with the supplies get the same share as those who fought, because the victory was the LORD's gift. The ruling bound every Israelite army from then on, "to this day." It answers a real problem of army life, and shows David acting as a king who gives law before he is king. Compare Numbers 31:27, where Moses splits the spoil between the fighters and the community.

settings.what: David's gifts to the elders of Judah
settings.to: the elders of Judah in Hebron and other towns where David had wandered
settings.when: on his return to Ziklag
settings.why: David sends part of the spoil as "a blessing" taken from the LORD's enemies. The gifts win the loyalty of the towns that will soon crown him at Hebron (2 Samuel 2:4). Readers can see faith and politics working together.

title: The Death of Saul
sum: On Mount Gilboa the Philistines rout Israel. Saul's sons Jonathan, Abinadab and Malchishua are killed. Saul, in anguish from the archers, asks his armor-bearer to kill him before the uncircumcised can abuse him. The armor-bearer refuses, and Saul falls on his own sword; the armor-bearer does the same. Israelites in the towns nearby abandon them, and the Philistines move in.

The next day the Philistines find the bodies. They cut off Saul's head, send the news through their land as good tidings to their idols, put his armor in the temple of the Ashtaroth, and fasten his body to the wall of Beth-shan. The men of Jabesh-gilead, whom Saul had rescued at the start of his reign, march all night, take down the bodies, burn them at Jabesh, bury the bones under a tamarisk, and fast seven days.
readings: Read as tragedy
Saul's story ends as it began, with Jabesh-gilead. Chosen, gifted, rejected, troubled, he dies by his own hand to avoid shame. Many readers find him the Bible's most tragic figure.
Read as judgment

Chronicles retells the chapter and adds the verdict: Saul died for his unfaithfulness, for not keeping the LORD's word and for consulting a ghost (1 Chronicles 10:13–14). Samuel's word at Endor comes true the next day.

views.H: The battle on Gilboa, about 1010 BC, ended Saul's reign and left the Philistines in control of the Jezreel Valley. Beth-shan was a fortified city at the valley's eastern end.
views.C: Critical scholars compare the different accounts of Saul's death (here, 2 Samuel 1:6–10 and 1 Chronicles 10) and see in 2 Samuel 1 a rival tradition or a story told to explain the Amalekite's claim.
views.L: The chapter is told with almost no comment. Echoes do the work: the head cut off as Goliath's was, the tamarisk where Saul once sat, and Jabesh, where his reign began.
views.J: The rabbis treated Saul's suicide as a special case, permitted because of the danger of torture and the shaming of Israel (Genesis Rabbah 34:13), and held that his death atoned for his sins (Berakhot 12b).
views.X: Christian readers have usually seen Saul as a warning: a gifted man who began well and ended in disobedience and despair. Augustine's teaching against suicide shaped later Christian judgment of his death.

deep.b: This chapter says Saul fell on his own sword. In 2 Samuel 1:6–10 an Amalekite tells David that he found Saul leaning on his spear, still alive, and killed him at Saul's request, bringing the crown and armlet as proof. Most readers think the Amalekite lied to win a reward: he found the body and invented the rest. Others think Saul's suicide attempt failed and the Amalekite finished it. First Chronicles 10 follows this chapter closely but adds that the Philistines fastened Saul's head in the temple of Dagon, and gives a theological verdict. The three accounts agree on the essentials: Saul died on Gilboa, by his own will, with his sons, at the hands of the Philistines.

Saul's first act as king was to rescue Jabesh-gilead from Nahash the Ammonite (11:1–11). His reign ends with the men of Jabesh risking their lives to rescue his body from disgrace. David will send them a blessing for this kindness (2 Samuel 2:5–6), using the word hesed, loyal love. Years later he will bring Saul's and Jonathan's bones from Jabesh and bury them in Benjamin, in Kish's tomb (2 Samuel 21:12–14). Whatever Saul's failures, the people he had saved did not forget him.
